# Files, directories, and OS

Sooner or later every program touches a file: reading configuration, writing a log, or listing a
directory. In many languages that work is spread across several libraries. Nim keeps it in one
module: `std/os`. This chapter uses that module for the tasks you will reach for most, and shows why
`import std/os` is not optional.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can split and rebuild file paths, write and then read a file, walk a
directory with stable output, read command-line arguments and environment variables, and read the
`undeclared identifier` message when a module is not imported.
:::

## One door: the `std/os` module

`std/os` covers file names, directories, arguments, and environment variables. We start with path
operations that never touch a file. Save the following as `main.nim`, then run
`nim c -r main.nim`.

```{.nim}
import std/os

let path = "/srv/app/logs/today.txt"
let (dir, name, ext) = splitFile(path)

echo "dir:  ", dir
echo "name: ", name
echo "ext:  ", ext
echo "back: ", joinPath(dir, name & ext)
```

```{.txt}
dir:  /srv/app/logs
name: today
ext:  .txt
back: /srv/app/logs/today.txt
```

`splitFile` breaks one path into three parts: directory, name, and extension. Notice that the
directory has no trailing separator. `joinPath` is the reverse: it joins the parts with the
separator the running system expects.

Path separators differ between Unix (`/`) and Windows (`\`). So do not glue paths with `&`. Use
`joinPath`, or the `/` operator the same module provides.

`splitFile` also works for a path with no directory: `splitFile("notes.txt")` yields an empty
directory. To take a single part, there are shortcuts: `extractFilename`, `parentDir`, and `tailDir`.
Reach for `splitFile` when you need two parts at once, and a shortcut when you need only one.

## Writing and reading a file

Two procedures cover most daily needs: `writeFile` and `readFile`.

```{.nim}
import std/[os, strutils]

let path = getTempDir() / "nim_id_files_demo.txt"

writeFile(path, "first line\nsecond line")

for line in readFile(path).splitLines():
  echo line

removeFile(path)
echo "exists after remove: ", fileExists(path)
```

```{.txt}
first line
second line
exists after remove: false
```

`writeFile` takes a path and a single string, and overwrites the file if it already exists.
`readFile` returns the whole contents as one string; the lines are split with `splitLines` from
`std/strutils`.

This example writes into `getTempDir()`, not the working directory. The reason is practical: the
example must run on any machine without leaving files in unexpected places. When it finishes,
`removeFile` deletes the file and `fileExists` proves it is gone. To create a directory, use
`createDir`; to test for one, `dirExists`.

If the file is missing, `readFile` does not return an error marker as in C. It raises `IOError`, and
the message carries the path it looked for. Nim is consistent here: an error you cannot ignore
becomes an exception, handled with `try` and `except` where the code knows what to do about it.

## Walking a directory

To list the contents of a directory, use `walkDir`. It yields a pair: the entry kind and its path.

```{.nim}
import std/[os, algorithm]

let dir = getTempDir() / "nim_id_walk_demo"
createDir(dir)
writeFile(dir / "b.txt", "second")
writeFile(dir / "a.txt", "first")

var names: seq[string]
for kind, path in walkDir(dir):
  names.add extractFilename(path)

sort names
for name in names:
  echo name

removeDir(dir)
```

```{.txt}
a.txt
b.txt
```

`walkDir` follows the file system order, which is not guaranteed. So the names are collected first,
then sorted with `sort` from `std/algorithm`. Without that step the output can differ on every run,
and an example whose output changes cannot be checked.

`kind` has type `PathComponent`. Its values include `pcFile`, `pcDir`, and two symlink variants. The
example ignores `kind`, but a `case` over it is the usual way to tell files from subdirectories.

`walkDir` does not descend into subdirectories; it reads one level. To traverse a whole directory
tree, use `walkDirRec`, which yields every file below the starting directory along with its path.

## Arguments and environment variables

Many small tools take their configuration from arguments and environment variables. Both live in
`std/os`.

```{.nim}
import std/os

echo "arguments: ", paramCount()

for i in 0 ..< paramCount():
  echo i, ": ", paramStr(i)
```

```{.txt}
arguments: 0
```

`paramCount()` counts the arguments after the program name, and `paramStr(i)` reads the `i`-th
argument, starting at zero. Run without arguments, the example prints zero. Run the resulting
binary with two extra arguments, and the loop prints both of them.

```{.nim}
import std/os

echo getEnv("NIM_ID_GREETING", "no greeting set")
```

```{.txt}
no greeting set
```

`getEnv` takes a variable name and a fallback value. If `NIM_ID_GREETING` is not set, the value used
is `"no greeting set"`. The fallback keeps the program from failing just because an environment
variable was never configured. When you need every argument as one sequence, `commandLineParams()`
returns them as a `seq[string]`.

## Deliberate error: forgetting to import `std/os`

The names above are not available by default. Forget `import std/os`, and the compiler stops on the
first line.

```{.nim}
echo getCurrentDir()
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(1, 6) Error: undeclared identifier: 'getCurrentDir'
```

Read it from the left. `main.nim` is the file. `(1, 6)` is line 1, column 6: the start of the
unknown name, just after `echo `. `undeclared identifier` means the name was used without ever being
declared or imported. The `candidates` line right below offers the closest names it knows.

The shortest fix: add `import std/os` on the first line. A useful habit, when the compiler names
something you were sure existed, is to check the `import` list first.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Print the file name and extension of the path `/etc/nim/nim.cfg` using `splitFile`.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/os

   echo splitFile("notes.txt").name
   ```
3. Write a program that writes two lines to a file in `getTempDir()`, reads it back, then prints the
   number of lines. Clean up the file at the end.
4. The code below fails. Fix it, then explain why:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/os

   if fileExists("/tmp") == "yes":
     echo "found"
   ```

## Summary

- `std/os` handles paths, files, directories, arguments, and environment variables.
- Build paths with `joinPath` or `/`, not with `&`, so the separator is right on every system.
- `readFile` and `writeFile` cover ordinary files; clean up temporary files after use.
- `walkDir` order is not guaranteed; sort yourself when the output must be stable.
- A missing `import std/os` gives an `undeclared identifier` at compile time, not a crash at runtime.
